extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of architecture, art history, and educated general readers interested in Venetian art, ornament, and political history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates aesthetic and historical standards for Venetian architecture and ornamentation—distinguishing styles, judging modifications, and describing proportional/constructional methods; also records related civic policies affecting religious orders. Intended as architectural criticism and guidance for appreciating or judging Venetian building-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renaissance families hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: There having been three principal styles of architecture in Venice,—the Greek or Byzantine, the Gothic, and the Renaissance, it will be shown, in the sequel, that the Renaissance itself is divided into three correspondent families: Renaissance engrafted on Byzantine, which is earliest and best; Renaissance engrafted on Gothic, which is second, and second best; Renaissance on Renaissance, which is double darkness, and worst of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy as an evaluative scale: prefer Renaissance work that is grafted on Byzantine precedents; treat Renaissance grafted on Gothic as inferior but acceptable; treat pure Renaissance-on-Renaissance pastiche as the worst. Examples and supporting discussion are given (see Ca' Trevisan, Ca' Dario).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Byzantine-engrafted Renaissance ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The palaces in which Renaissance is engrafted on Byzantine are characterized by an ornamentation very closely resembling, and in some cases identical with, early Byzantine work; namely, groups of colored marble circles inclosed in interlacing bands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor ornament that preserves Byzantine feeling: inlaid colored-marbles, interlacing bands, careful treatment of animals and foliage, and delicate finishing. Specific examples (Ca' Trevisan, Ca' Dario) illustrate proportion, color, and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical proportion in design
rubrics_metrics.description: If we take five circles in geometrical proportion, each diameter being two-thirds of the diameter next above it, and arrange the circles so proportioned, in contact with each other, ... we shall find that an increase quite imperceptible in the diameter of the circles in the angles, will enable us to inscribe the whole in a square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple geometric constructions (e.g., nested circles with consistent diameter ratios) to derive harmonious ornament proportions. Confirm proportions by eye-sketching and by aligning design lines with band centers; geometry yields pleasing, structurally sound ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding spoiled or composite orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite, which is Ionic and Corinthian mixed, is one of the worst of ten thousand forms referable to the Corinthian as their head: it may be described as a spoiled Corinthian. Tuscan (no order at all, but a spoiled Doric) and Roman Doric (Doric more spoiled) are simply among the most stupid variations ever invented upon forms already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hybrid or degraded 'orders' skeptically; prefer clarity and fidelity to the genuine classical orders rather than inventing confused or 'spoiled' hybrids. Multiplication of orders often signals confusion rather than improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ionic as agreeable extravagance (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ionic...the idea was taken (Vitruvius says) from a woman's hair, curled; but its lateral processes look more like rams' horns: be that as it may, it is a mere piece of agreeable extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Ionic ornament as playful or decorative rather than rigidly canonical; it can be adapted, but beware that arbitrary substitutions (ibex horns, ass heads, etc.) create numerous fanciful 'orders' and undermine architectural seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only two great orders (essential distinctions matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are in very deed only two orders, of which the Greek, Doric, and Corinthian are the first examples, and they not perfect, nor in anywise sufficiently representative of the vast families to which they belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus criticism on the essential distinctions between the two great order-families (explained in referenced chapters). Do not treat minor named variants as equal authorities; study foundational distinctions to judge later variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess schools by impetuosity vs refinement (Northern energy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The differences in all these schools are more in the degrees of their impetuosity and refinement (these qualities being, in most cases, in inverse ratio, yet much muted by the Arabs) than in the style of the ornaments they employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating regional or historic schools, weigh their relative impetuosity (force, vigor) against their refinement (subtlety, finish). Similar motifs may appear across cultures; the degree and treatment determine character and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of animals and symbolic motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also much Byzantine feeling in the treatment of the animals, especially in the two birds of the lower compartment...The dove, alighted, with the olive-branch plucked off, is opposed to the raven with restless expanded wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the rendering and symbolism of animals and motifs: their attitude, finish, and relation to surrounding ornament contribute to stylistic authenticity. Color choices (e.g., green and white marbles) and exquisite finishing are important markers of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: State controls on religious orders (Jesuit limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decree which permitted their establishment in Venice required formal renewal every three years; that no Jesuit could stay in Venice more than three years; that the slightest disobedience to the authority of the government was instantly punished by imprisonment; that no Venetian could enter the order without express permission from the government; that the notaries were forbidden to sanction any testamentary disposal of property to the Jesuits; finally, that the heads of noble families were forbidden to permit their children to be educated in the Jesuits' colleges, on pain of degradation from their rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural restrictions are cited as examples of how the state tightly regulated religious influence; they function as criteria for judging the relationship between civic authority and religious institutions in historical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of lay and clerical officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Venetians accomplished therein what we ridiculously call a separation of 'Church and State'...they ought to call a separation of lay and clerical officers. The enforcement of absolute exclusion of the clergy from the councils of the state...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this separation as an analytical standard when evaluating Venetian governance: its effects (both practical and moral) are discussed—neither unambiguously praised nor condemned—so weigh intended security against potential loss of religious element in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy of religious tolerance maintained by policing
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only subjects of the religion Greek conserved their exercise, but the Protestants, the Armenians, the Mahometans, the Jews, all the religions, all the sects...had temples, and the sepulture in the churches was not refused to heretics. A vigilant police applied with the same care to extinguish the discord, and to prevent the fanatics and novatores from troubling the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Venice's tolerance not merely by presence of multiple religious communities but by the active civic measures (vigilant policing, suppression of disorders) that maintained public order; tolerance is presented as pragmatic and state-managed.
